title: AI-prefilled organizers and automated chasing for missing client documents
problem: Collecting client documents means repeated emails and late files, and returns claiming certain credits also need a documented preparer interview and Form 8867.
approach: Canopy's Smart Intake offers AI-prefilled organizers that clients confirm or change, plus document request lists and AI file classification.
Canopy says firms can save as much as 20 minutes per client (vendor-published).
Basis and ApariPro describe agents or automation that spot data gaps and contact clients; Columbia's TaxBench is still in development.
Staff review open items, and the preparer conducts the due-diligence interview and signs Form 8867.

title: AI reads tax source documents and K-1 footnotes, flagging exceptions for review
problem: K-1 packages and multi-tier partnerships defeat template scanning and manual keying, and an extraction error can flow into a return without any flag.
approach: CCH Axcess Scan (Wolters Kluwer) classifies and extracts tax documents, surfacing only exceptions; PwC agents state a confidence level per K-1 footnote.
Wolters Kluwer says K-1 extraction averages 97.5% overall accuracy (vendor-published); PwC says one person now reviews where three used to gather (self-reported).
Reviewers override low-confidence mappings with a recorded reason and compare extracted figures to source documents.
Complex or ambiguous documents escalate to senior review.

title: Retail tax offices use AI to cut data entry and free time
problem: Preparers in assisted-tax offices spend much of an appointment collecting and entering information, leaving less time for advice.
approach: H&R Block management said it is using AI to eliminate manual data entry and automate initial prior-year return review.
The pilot is to expand to a full designated market area for tax season 27.
H&R Block reported higher client satisfaction in the pilot model, with no figures given (self-reported).
Tax pros remain responsible for the returns and the client guidance.

title: Agent drafts a simple personal tax return from documents for CPA review
problem: Preparing even simple 1040s means sorting documents and keying data by hand, which crowds out higher-value work in a short season.
approach: Thomson Reuters' Ready to Review agents process source documents and prior-year returns and draft returns with source links, two-year comparisons and diagnostics.
Announced with an early-adopter program, and later said to be generally available in the US from 15 Dec 2025.
A CLH CPAs partner said it saves about an hour per simple 1040 (vendor-published).
A professional reviews the draft before delivery, and the taxpayer reviews the return before signing.
who: Thomson Reuters, CLH CPAs and Consultants

title: Agents prepare complex individual returns end to end for CPA sign-off
problem: Complex returns with many K-1s, brokerage statements and multiple states take days of preparer and reviewer time while firms are short of staff.
approach: Black Ore, Accrual (Armanino) and Basis agents extract data, apply tax logic, build workpapers and route returns into firm software.
OpenAI says Tax AI saves about a third of preparation time (vendor-published); Black Ore claims accuracy above 99 percent (vendor-published).
Boulay partner says returns with 60 or 70-plus K-1s fell from over 100 hours to about 15-20 (vendor-published).
A CPA reviews and signs off before the return reaches the client and the IRS.
who: Black Ore, Basis, Accrual, OpenAI, Crete

title: Agent prepares partnership, S corporation and trust returns through K-1s for review
problem: Partnership and trust returns need trial-balance import, allocations, depreciation, basis tracking and K-1 tie-out, much of it in spreadsheets, multiplying the review burden.
approach: Accrual describes preparing partnership returns from trial balance to partner K-1s (Armanino is a customer); Basis demonstrated an agent completing a 1065.
Armanino statistics show 86.5% of draft values matching the final return and an estimated 50% less federal effort (vendor-published).
Accrual shows proposed changes and asks for approval before applying them.
A practitioner reviews the draft and signs.

title: Trial balance to tax workpapers for partnership and S corporation returns
problem: Business returns start with mapping the client's trial balance to return lines and building book-to-tax and fixed-asset workpapers by hand.
approach: Basis says its agents map client accounts to return lines, flag unmapped accounts and draft book-to-tax and fixed-asset workpapers.
A Whitcomb & Sheridan partner says a two-to-three-hour task takes about 30 minutes; the quote is general (vendor-published).
Staff review mapping exceptions and workpaper drafts.

title: Agent works inside the firm's own tax software and documents each entry
problem: Pre-preparation tools push data into the tax engine, so the firm still does the final steps by hand; WCG wants AI working inside its software.
approach: TaxGPT launched an agent that signs in to the firm's tax software, enters data, clears diagnostics and documents each entry to source.
TaxGPT claims a 50% cut in first-pass preparation time on its product page and 90% in its launch release (vendor-published).
The firm's team reviews and signs off, and its software stays the system of record.

title: General-purpose agents run practitioner-taught routines and build return workpapers
problem: Following up across call notes, open issues, binders and signature requests on a return is done by hand across several systems.
approach: Accrual's Arc, unveiled 9 Sep 2026, drafts a plan and, once approved, executes across firm systems with an audit trail.
A practitioner, Sam Leon, uses Claude Cowork to prepare returns; the episode title says 5x faster (self-reported).
The practitioner approves the plan and each proposed change.

title: Idea: deterministic tax engine calculates returns; language model handles intake
problem: Idea, not a deployment: unaided language models calculate returns unreliably, and calculation errors, wrong tax tables and eligibility mistakes are costly and hard to audit.
approach: Idea from researchers: pair the model with a deterministic calculation engine or symbolic solver; TaxCalcBench authors see a continued need for engines.
On 51 simplified cases the best of four models computed 32.35% of returns correctly under the strict test (published benchmark).
The preparer would review the engine-calculated return and any model-supplied inputs.
who: Columbia DAP Lab, Column Tax, Johns Hopkins researchers

title: Grounded assistant helps preparers with tax changes and return positions, authorities verified
problem: Preparers must stay current on tax changes and answer unusual questions, and general AI models can invent authorities, as a 2026 Tax Court case showed.
approach: H&R Block and OpenAI said in April 2025 they were developing a tool grounded in vetted data; management called Sidekick adoption strong.
No usage counts or accuracy figures were published (self-reported).
The tax pro decides the answer; a reviewer opens and reads each cited authority.

title: AI-assisted return review with source tie-out, diagnostics and audit-sensitive flags
problem: Review becomes the bottleneck when preparation speeds up, and reviewers must catch extraction, mapping and eligibility errors across more returns.
approach: Intuit ProConnect runs an AI assistant against thousands of diagnostics; Basis, Accrual, Thomson Reuters, TaxGPT and Filed trace figures and flag exceptions.
Filed's sample report claims fixing a wage mapping restores a $54,861 deduction for an illustrative client (vendor-published).
Reviewers inspect flagged items, also sample unflagged ones against source, and the preparer or reviewer signs.
who: Intuit, Basis, Accrual, Thomson Reuters, Filed

title: Idea: review controls for AI-assisted returns, with decision logs and override monitoring
problem: Idea, not a deployment: AI-assisted volume dilutes partner review, and a firm without records cannot show what the tool suggested and what the preparer verified.
approach: Idea from published guidance: log every AI suggestion and the preparer's decision with override rationale, and review override rates by preparer monthly.
Scale sampling to volume and escalate novel or uncertain positions to senior review regardless of the AI's confidence.
Australia's tax practitioners board and the IRS OPR expect AI procedures to be verified and documented.

title: Automated look-back review of prior-year returns offered to every new client
problem: Second Look, which reviews a new client's last three years of returns for missed opportunities, was manual, so tax pros rarely offered it to new clients.
approach: H&R Block management said it automated Second Look over about 18 months with newer AI, so many more new clients opt in.
Clients who received Second Look returned at a rate over 600 basis points higher, an uncontrolled comparison (self-reported).
Tax pros focus on the returns with the greatest opportunity.

title: AI-drafted client updates, return explanations and plan comparisons, reviewed before sending
problem: Clients call to ask where their return stands, preparers write explanations by hand, and firms cannot paste client data into public AI tools.
approach: Status messages are generated when a job changes stage; practitioners use AI to draft correspondence; Intuit lists an AI Client Briefing.
WCG says it will use a SOC 2-compliant, zero-data-retention sandbox to turn returns into client narratives, quotes and tax-plan comparisons.
The preparer reads and edits every client communication before sending.

title: Automated return delivery, e-signature and Form 8879 e-file authorisation
problem: Assembling the return package, collecting signatures including Form 8879 from more than one signer, and taking payment are manual and error-prone.
approach: Thomson Reuters names SafeSend and SurePrep as delivery and e-signature tools, with the vendor claiming an AI layer that flags discrepancies.
Thomson Reuters says firms using SafeSend save about 15 minutes on every return (vendor-published).
The preparer signs the return, and the taxpayer reviews it before signing Form 8879.

title: UK self assessment and Making Tax Digital returns with AI document processing
problem: UK firms chase clients, review documents manually and re-key data into tax software for self assessment returns and quarterly Making Tax Digital submissions.
approach: ApariPro says it automates client information collection, AI document processing, return population and submission, integrating with Wolters Kluwer's CCH iFirm.
No figures are published; anonymous testimonials say manual data entry fell (vendor-published).
The team reviews and approves all information before submission.

title: Phased adoption: simple returns first, scope gates and parallel runs before scaling
problem: Firms adopt on vendor claims and cannot say whether time, quality or cycle time improved, and one proposed tool had no scope limits or phase boundary.
approach: Practitioners advise starting AI preparation on simple returns and running last year's returns through the product to compare with what was filed.
Werfel's case study (an idea) authorises tools in phases, with gates such as a hallucination rate of 2% or less.
No firm has published a parallel-run or phased-rollout result (self-reported).

title: Firm AI policy, approved-tool list and vendor due diligence for tax practices
problem: Staff use AI tools whether sanctioned or not, nobody owns AI, and firms cannot show how outputs were verified while handling highly sensitive return data.
approach: IRS Office of Professional Responsibility says firms should adopt AI policies covering training, data handling and accuracy monitoring, and vet vendors.
A Journal of Accountancy article recommends approved-tool lists, an AI lead and documenting prompts and verification in the client file.
Thomson Reuters reports more than one-third of professionals use AI tools their firm has not sanctioned (vendor-published).
A principal or AI committee approves tools and use cases before use on client work.
who: IRS OPR, Thomson Reuters, Wolters Kluwer

title: AI pod, champion network and competence training that protects the junior pipeline
problem: Tools change faster than firm processes, regulators make AI competence personal, and AI automates entry-level tasks that juniors learn from.
approach: PwC reports a governance committee, an Agent OS managing agent tools, more than 3,200 AI champions and a My AI training programme.
PwC reports more than 350,000 training hours in the US firm; these are enablement measures, not tax outcomes (self-reported).
WCG says its AI Tax Prep Pod launches in November 2026 to test tools and document best practices.

title: Client disclosure and section 7216 consent before AI touches return information
problem: Written consent rules may apply before AI tools use return information, whether an AI tool counts as software or a third party is unsettled, and no disclosure rule was found.
approach: Practitioners and the AICPA advise a signed stand-alone AI consent, an inventory of AI tools touching client data and AI governance.
Other guidance suggests engagement-letter wording on AI use; Australia's regulator says permission may be given in a signed engagement letter.
The client signs and dates consent before any disclosure; counsel reviews the language before the tool is used.

title: Idea: reprice return work from hours to value as AI shortens preparation
problem: Idea, not a deployment: hours-times-rate billing shrinks when AI cuts preparation time, and the IRS OPR says billing for time not spent may breach fee rules.
approach: Idea under dispute: price by value, bundle return preparation with advisory services, and disclose and credit AI efficiencies as OPR describes.
The AICPA says OPR's language does not appear to allow value pricing and is not authoritative; it is working with the IRS.
The partner approves the fee basis and the client agrees it in the engagement letter.

title: Replace offshore or contract data entry and first-pass preparation with AI-prepared returns
problem: Busy-season volume is met with outsourced and offshore preparers, raising onboarding, quality and disclosure concerns amid a labour shortage.
approach: Firms bring first-pass preparation onshore through AI products instead of staffing it offshore or with contractors.
A vendor founder says users of his agent talk about bringing work back onshore; no outcome figures are published.
A partner reviews the AI-prepared return.

title: AI-native roll-ups acquire small tax practices and run them on in-house AI
problem: Small tax practices carry heavy manual workloads and thin margins and struggle to adopt new processes, while buyers seek recurring-revenue service businesses.
approach: Multiplier acquired Citrine International Tax, a 12-person boutique, and applied AI tools it built in-house; Aardvark Tax Advisors describes itself as AI-native.
TechCrunch reports Multiplier's AI tools helped Citrine more than double its profit margins (self-reported).
At Aardvark, a signing practitioner decides what needs human review and when a return is ready for signature.

title: Taxpayer-side AI agents draft or check returns, bypassing or second-guessing the preparer
problem: Self-filers face cost, time and jargon and some now ask general-purpose AI for help instead of hiring a preparer.
approach: Perplexity announced Computer for Taxes on 2 Apr 2026: it reviews uploaded documents, asks questions and drafts a federal return.
A TaxSlayer test of four chatbots found refund errors averaging more than $2,000 across eight scenarios (vendor-published).
No checkpoint by design for self-filers; practitioners are asked to validate client-brought AI conclusions.

title: Reasonable-compensation study for S corporation owners built duty by duty
problem: S corporation owners must pay themselves reasonable wages with no specific guidelines, and a custom study has been a costly one-off engagement.
approach: Instead lists a reasonable compensation agent workflow; WageProof prices each owner duty with Bureau of Labor Statistics data and names every source.
WageProof says a client report takes about 15 minutes (vendor-published); its founder says chatbot wage citations often did not check out.
The preparer confirms duty matches and a reviewer checks every wage figure traces to a source.

title: Shareholder and partner basis schedules computed from the return, with negative-basis alerts
problem: Reviewers of S corporation and partnership returns must confirm shareholder basis, capital accounts and debt effects, which are error-prone to build by hand.
approach: Instead says its S corporation agent includes basis calculations and K-1 generation; Intuit Tax Advisor alerts when distributions produce negative basis.
Thomson Reuters says CoCounsel Tax can work through passive activity limits and at-risk basis with a source for every answer.
The preparer agrees opening basis to source records, and the reviewer signs off negative or restored basis.

title: One AI agent per client holds every entity they own
problem: Owner-managed clients can have a personal return, operating entities and a trust, each prepared and reviewed as its own return.
approach: Instead assigns each client an entity agent that indexes uploaded documents, holds filing history, carryforwards and elections, and flags year-over-year changes.
Instead says the agent understands how a client's 1040, 1120-S and 1065 interact; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).
The preparer confirms the ownership map and that each K-1 ties to the issuing entity return.

title: Quarterly estimated-tax projections for owners with safe-harbor analysis
problem: Owners of S corporations and partnerships pay estimated tax on flow-through income, and no source describes how firms build these projections today.
approach: Instead lists quarterly federal and state estimated-tax calculations for shareholders, including safe-harbor analysis and flow-through impact.
Instead also lists a ready-to-run workflow called Build shareholder tax estimates (vendor-published); no outcome figures are given.
The preparer reviews projection assumptions before the owner is told what to pay.

title: AI-native platform replaces the firm's tax engine and e-files entity returns
problem: WCG describes a reset risk: an AI preparing a return in its own software cannot hand a half-finished return to the firm's tax software.
approach: On 2026-05-08 Instead announced it completed government e-file testing for five return types, and says it can replace legacy tax software.
Instead says it cuts complex return preparation from 4-6 hours to under 60 minutes (vendor-published).
The CPA signs, and the reviewer works from the tool's workpapers.

title: Estate, gift and fiduciary returns prepared by agents from governing documents
problem: Some preparers are expanding into estate work, yet no source describes AI preparing estate or gift returns in a firm.
approach: Instead lists fiduciary 1041 returns among entity types its agent covers and lists 706 and 709 as Coming 2026.
Thomson Reuters' fiduciary software descriptions did not describe an AI function; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).
The preparer reads the governing instrument against the draft allocation to beneficiaries.
